_comment: SKELETON permission allowlist for GATEWAY TURNS ONLY (KTD12).
Copy it to the path named by `permissions.settings_file` in the instance
config and EDIT it: the `allow` array below carries only the two rules that
are true for every instance. Nothing here knows what YOUR agent runs.
Passed via `claude -p --settings <file>` by turn_runner; it is NOT
.claude/settings.json, so it never affects your interactive sessions in the
same repo.
Why an allowlist instead of --dangerously-skip-permissions: a headless turn
cannot answer a prompt, and circuit-breaker prompts (rm -rf /) still fire
under bypass -- that would hang the turn forever while it holds the session
flock. bypass is also refused when running as root, which breaks portability
to other machines. Under dontAsk there are no prompts and no hang, which is
the behavior we want. NOTE: an earlier version of this comment claimed
'anything not allowed below fails' -- that is FALSE and cost us; see FILE
SCOPE below. dontAsk gates Bash, but NOT Read/Write/Edit/WebSearch.
WHAT TO ADD, and it is the step people skip and regret:
- every command the instance's CLAUDE.md tells the brain to run, with the
interpreter written as a LITERAL absolute path, e.g.
Bash(~/.local/share/<instance-name>/venv/bin/python3 -c *)
Bash(~/.local/share/<instance-name>/venv/bin/python3 scripts/<tool>.py *)
One rule per script is deliberate -- a single wildcard over the whole
scripts/ directory allows whatever lands there later.
- anything it writes outside ./state/**.
MCP tools are NOT gated by this file: `dontAsk` gates them, but membership
comes from the instance's `permissions.mcp_config`, so adding a server there
is what grants it -- not a rule here.
VERIFIED 2026-07-28 against real turns. Two findings shaped these rules:
(a) A command containing SHELL-VARIABLE EXPANSION is denied regardless of
the allowlist -- the matcher cannot know what $PY expands to. CLAUDE.md
therefore tells the brain to write this interpreter path literally.
(b) The tilde form matched a real invocation; the same rule written with
the expanded /Users/... path did NOT. Keep the tilde form, and keep
rule and command spelled the same way.
FILE SCOPE (measured 2026-07-31, and it corrected a wrong assumption):
`dontAsk` does NOT gate the Read tool. A probe turn read /etc/hosts and
~/.zshrc despite `Read(./**)` being the only Read rule -- so the allow list
never confined reads, and the home dotfiles (which hold live tokens in
plaintext) were reachable from every turn. WebSearch is likewise ungated:
it works with no rule at all.
There is NO 'deny everything except the workdir'. Deny beats allow
unconditionally: `deny Read(//**)` + `allow Read(./**)` denies the workdir
too (verified -- even ./config.yaml came back DENIED). So confinement here
is a targeted DENY list of the places worth protecting, which is
whack-a-mole by construction. Add to it rather than assuming a default.
WHY THERE IS NO Write(...) RULE ANYWHERE IN THIS FILE, on either side.
MEASURED 2026-08-03 with four probe turns under `dontAsk`, because the
reasoning that says you need them is genuinely persuasive and wrong: Edit
requires an existing file and Write creates one, so `deny Edit(~/.ssh/**)`
*looks* like it would leave a turn free to create authorized_keys, and
`deny Edit(~/Library/LaunchAgents/**)` free to drop a new plist -- both
persistent-backdoor primitives on a machine where this plugin installs
launchd jobs. What the probes actually found:
1. deny Write(~/probe/**), no Edit rule -> the CLI prints, per rule and on
EVERY turn's stderr whether or not a file tool is used: 'Write(...) is
not matched by file permission checks -- only Edit(path) rules are.
Use Edit(...) instead (Edit rules cover all file-editing tools).'
A Write(...) rule is inert on BOTH sides, and 19 of them would mean 19
warning lines in every turn's log.
2. allow Edit(~/probe/**), no deny -> the Write tool CREATED a new file
there. Edit rules do cover creation.
3. allow + deny Edit(~/probe/**) -> the Write tool was DENIED and no file
appeared. So `deny Edit(<path>)` blocks creation as well as editing.
The gap the Write rules were guarding does not exist; the rules guarding it
did nothing. `Edit(<path>)` on the deny side is the whole protection, and
the same fact is why `Edit(./state/**)` alone is enough on the allow side
for the nightly rotation to write the handoff.
HONEST SCOPE: this is not a sandbox. The brain legitimately runs inline
python (`python3 -c ...`), so allowing it is equivalent to allowing arbitrary
code. What this list actually buys: no prompts, no headless hang, portability
off this machine, and a deny-list for the few genuinely destructive verbs.
The real security boundary remains the owner-gated transport plus the
owner-allowlisted send path, not this file.
MAINTENANCE: a missing rule does NOT fail the turn -- verified 2026-07-28:
the turn exits 0 and the model narrates the denial. The turn runner therefore
treats send-evidence, not exit status, as delivery truth. The parity suite in
--real mode runs real turns and is the gate that proves this list complete.
That gate earned its keep immediately: the rotation drill caught Edit being
allowed on the handoff file ALONE while Write was allowed on all of
state/** -- an arbitrary split, since the model picks Edit for a file that
already exists. The nightly flush edits an existing file, so the split would
eventually have silently dropped a night of context (rotation is silent, so
there is no send-evidence to catch it; rotate() now verifies the file's
mtime instead). One rule over the whole of state/** replaced the split.
